paras: The attempted lynching of John Taylor at Greensboro took place on the night of Monday, June 6, 1881, when, according to the Raleigh Observer, a large party of armed men rode into Greensboro, North Carolina, to take Taylor, a Black prisoner, from the Guilford County jail. Taylor was accused of raping a white woman, Mrs. James Irwin, near Reidsville in Rockingham County, and the sheriff removed him from the jail before the men could reach him. The attempt followed a raid on the Rockingham County jail at Wentworth, and five days later a larger party broke into the Greensboro jail, took Taylor out and hanged him.

The Charlotte Democrat reported that on Friday night, June 3, two Black farm hands employed by Col. James Irwin, John Taylor and George Gunn, went to the Irwin house near Reidsville while Irwin and his daughter were away, and that Taylor assaulted Mrs. Irwin. The Winston Western Sentinel printed the two names as Jim Taylor and Bob Green. Both men were arrested the next day, reportedly confessed before a justice at Reidsville, and were committed to the jail at Wentworth while lynching was "freely talked of."

Warned that a party meant to take the prisoners, Rockingham sheriff Johnston left Wentworth with Taylor and, changing his route toward Kernersville, handed him to O. C. Wheeler, the Guilford County jailer, who lodged him in the Greensboro jail. The Charlotte Democrat placed the Wentworth raid on Sunday night, June 5, saying the men forced the jail doors, found Taylor gone, left Gunn behind and rode after the sheriff. The Yorkville Enquirer instead dated the gathering at Wentworth to Saturday night and said the sheriff kept Taylor at Kernersville overnight and brought him to Greensboro on Monday morning.

On Monday night, a gentleman told the Raleigh Observer, "a large party of armed men rode into Greensboro to take the negro fiend from the jail there, but he was taken away by the Sheriff and escaped death then." The Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic said in its first report that Taylor "was pursued all the way thither, but again fled to safer quarters," and a week later wrote that "Judge Lynch" followed him to Greensboro but, failing to find him, dispersed.

The Yorkville Enquirer gave a fuller version in which the sheriff of Guilford County was told that an armed mob would try that night to take Taylor from the jail and hang him. To prevent violence, by this account, the sheriff took Taylor under guard to "a safe place near Greensboro," kept him there until Tuesday morning and then returned him to his cell. No report in the coverage describes the men entering the jail that night, and no one was reported hurt.

Taylor remained in the Greensboro jail until Saturday night, June 11, when, during an eclipse of the moon, a body of men who had met five miles north of town demanded the keys from Wheeler, cut through three locked doors and took Taylor, who was chained to the floor. They carried him toward Reidsville tied to the back of a buggy and hanged him from an oak at about 4 a.m. on Sunday, some seven miles from Reidsville. A coroner's jury found that he had been hanged by unknown parties, and he was buried at the foot of the tree at a county cost of $4. Estimates of the lynching party ran from 50 or 60 to about 200 men.

Gunn, about whose guilt the Farmer and Mechanic said there was "some doubt," remained in the Rockingham jail awaiting a regular trial, and no report of his trial or of any prosecution of either party of lynchers was found. The Charlotte Democrat added that "the colored people of that section" were said to consider that Taylor "got his just deserts."

The Monday-night attempt appeared only in North and South Carolina papers, as a paragraph within longer accounts of the assault and of Taylor's flight from Wentworth. These papers stated the accusation as fact, called Taylor a "fiend," a "devil" and a "brute," and treated the sheriff's protection of him as an obstacle to punishment. The Western Sentinel wrote that "the courts should not be bothered with her outragers," and the Farmer and Mechanic followed its account of the sheriff's escape with "It is a great pity!" and a remark that "the good lessons taught by the Ku Klux in 1871 are forgotten in 1881."

After the lynching, the Farmer and Mechanic headlined its account "Dead and Done For! Decently and in Order!" and regretted only "the delay," while the Greensboro Battle Ground, as reprinted in Hillsborough, would have preferred that the law take its course but thought the lynchers "will not be blamed much." The lynching itself went out by telegraph from Danville, Virginia, and ran in papers in Georgia, West Virginia, Delaware, Texas, Arkansas and Ohio, often under headlines about the eclipse; the Wheeling Register called the lynchers "Virginia Vigilantes." None of these out-of-state reports mentioned the earlier attempt at Greensboro.

Accounts differ on whether the men of June 6 actually reached Greensboro: the Raleigh Observer's informant and the Farmer and Mechanic said they rode into or followed Taylor to the town. The Yorkville Enquirer, by contrast, reported only that the sheriff was warned of a planned attempt and hid his prisoner. The papers also differ on which sheriff moved Taylor that night, the Farmer and Mechanic implying the Rockingham sheriff who had brought him and the Yorkville Enquirer naming the sheriff of Guilford.
According to the Charlotte Democrat, Taylor said in the Greensboro jail that Gunn was the guilty man, while acknowledging that the two had agreed to go to the house together.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of John Taylor at Greensboro
bases: An armed party sought to take a jailed Black prisoner from the Greensboro jail and hang him, and was thwarted when the sheriff removed him (A3, A8, A9).

On June 6 a 'large party of armed men' sought to take Taylor from jail to hang him for an alleged rape, but he was removed and 'escaped death then' (A3, A8); the same prisoner was taken from the same jail and hanged on June 11-12 (A10, A12), which is the completed lynching and is recorded separately.

The Raleigh Observer (A3), both Farmer and Mechanic reports (A1, A9) and the Yorkville Enquirer (A8) agree that a mob sought Taylor at Greensboro on or about Monday, June 6, and that he was spirited away, though they differ on whether the men actually reached the town.

accounts.gist: A 'large party of armed men' rode into Greensboro on Monday night to take Taylor from the jail, but the sheriff had taken him away and he 'escaped death then'.

accounts.label: Farmer and Mechanic (Raleigh)
accounts.gist: Taylor was pursued from Rockingham to Greensboro; the lynchers followed but, failing to find him, dispersed until Saturday night.

accounts.label: Yorkville Enquirer
accounts.gist: The sheriff of Guilford was informed that an armed mob would try to take Taylor that night and hang him, so he took Taylor under guard to a safe place near Greensboro until Tuesday morning; no arrival of the mob is described.

framing.detail: The Farmer and Mechanic followed the escape with 'It is a great pity!' and a remark about forgotten Ku Klux 'lessons', and later headlined the lynching 'Dead and Done For! Decently and in Order!', regretting only 'the delay'.
The Western Sentinel said 'the courts should not be bothered with her outragers'.
The Charlotte Democrat called Taylor a 'negro fiend' and 'devils in human form' and expected a quick trial at the sitting Superior Court.
The Yorkville Enquirer narrated the sheriff's precaution matter-of-factly while calling the delay a postponement of 'the vengeance of an infuriated people'.
Out-of-state papers carried only the June 11 lynching, as a Danville wire under eclipse and 'Judge Lynch' headlines.
